title: Angles
capsule: The Angles were a Germanic people originating in the Angeln peninsula on the Baltic coast of Schleswig-Holstein, first attested by Tacitus around AD 98 as settled near the River Elbe beyond the Semnones and Langobards. During the fifth century, Angle warriors and settlers crossed the North Sea in the wave of migrations that followed Roman Britain's collapse, establishing dominant kingdoms in Northumbria, Mercia, and East Anglia. Their cultural imprint proved decisive: the name England derives from Engla land — 'land of the Angles' — and the Old English language itself bears their tribal name. By the late sixth century the Angles had effectively ceased to exist as a distinct continental people, their Jutland homeland largely abandoned according to Bede.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The continental Angles are documented only by Tacitus and Ptolemy, with no surviving material culture definitively assigned to them in Angeln; the migration chronology (broadly fifth century) rests on Bede and archaeological inference rather than contemporary records, making precise territorial mapping speculative.
